considered.reasoning: This reverses the usual framing — the interaction is between financing intensity and the absence of real investment — so it tests a mechanism no prior archive signal touches and is not a restatement of externally funded expansion. Cash holdings and the issuance-to-cash channel are orthogonal to CMA and RMW, giving the FF5 spread a chance to survive factor adjustment. Both legs are high-coverage and the deployment leg is demeaned, so heavy issuers who genuinely invest score near zero rather than being lumped with hoarders.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LeveredCapexOverhang
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(lt, at), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The marginal project financed with new debt by an already highly levered firm is a risk-shifting bet made on behalf of creditors, not a positive-NPV investment; capital spending is therefore most damaging where both the stock and the flow of debt financing are high.
considered.reasoning: Unlike the gen-0 designs, the financing state here combines the level of total liabilities with the incremental debt flow, so it identifies constrained, overhung expanders rather than simply active issuers — a distress-adjacent dimension only partly captured by HML and RMW. Capex is scaled by assets and enters as a bounded rank weight, and the financing composite is demeaned, so unlevered self-funded capex sits at the short end of the sort. All inputs are balance-sheet items, so coverage and decile membership should be far more stable than the 0.10-coverage gen-0 portfolios.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PostLeverageRetrenchment
considered.hypothesis: The informative moment in externally funded expansion is the hangover: a firm that levered up last year and is now cutting its reinvestment rate has revealed that the financed projects failed, leaving the debt service without the growth, and the market is slow to mark this down.
considered.reasoning: This is a genuine timing test rather than a horizon variant — prior-year leverage-increasing financing is interacted with the current-year change in the reinvestment rate, so it fires on retrenchment after financing, not on contemporaneous expansion. Because the long leg contains shrinking investors rather than aggressive growers, its CMA and HML loadings differ sharply from every gen-0 signal, which is precisely the exposure profile needed for the raw spread to survive FF5 adjustment. The demeaned lagged financing leg ensures that firms cutting capex without prior leverage build-up score near zero.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BookEquityPerShareBackedExpansion
considered.hypothesis: Capacity expansion is value-creating when the equity base is being built from retained earnings rather than from new shareholders: book equity per share rising alongside the capital stock, with the firm simultaneously able to raise its dividend, proves the expansion is paid for out of realized profits, whereas identical expansion accompanied by falling equity per share and a dividend cut reveals dependence on outside capital and funding stress.
considered.reasoning: The funding leg is no longer share-count growth or a payout level — it is the growth in book equity per share, which differences dilution against equity accretion and is therefore a measure of internally generated capital, plus the change in the dividend rate as a Lintner-style commitment signal; neither channel restates net share issuance or net payout yield, and the combination avoids the point mass that a dividend-change-only leg would create for non-payers. Interacting this with gross PP&E growth rather than an assets-based investment ratio keeps the object of investment concrete (installed capacity) and distinguishes the test from the already-evaluated investment-times-payout structure, whose funding leg had no internal-accretion content. Because the demeaned funding leg contributes zero at the cross-sectional median, the sort compares equally expanding firms whose expansion is self-financed against those whose expansion is externally financed, so CMA exposure largely cancels in the spread while the retained-earnings dimension is unpriced by FF5.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: IndAdjLeverageStretchedReinvestment
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, ppent), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(lt, at), 1)), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A high reinvestment rate is most damaging when the firm is already levered beyond its industry norm and is still drawing new debt: the marginal project is a creditor-financed bet whose downside accrues to equity only after the debt is serviced, so expected equity returns fall relative to identically investing but unlevered peers.
considered.reasoning: This directly refines the only archive signal with a correctly signed FF5 alpha (LeveredCapexOverhang) by fixing its diagnosed weakness — the raw lt/at level dominated the composite and sorted on industry distress, so leverage is now industry-z-scored, leaving firm-specific balance-sheet stretch while retaining the debt-flow channel. Scaling capex by installed capital (ppent) makes the investment leg a reinvestment rate rather than an asset-growth proxy, further separating the sort from CMA. The demeaned financing composite means average-leverage firms contribute zero regardless of reinvestment rate, so the spread is an interaction test rather than a capex sort.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ShortDebtFundedCapacity
considered.hypothesis: Funding long-lived physical capacity with short-maturity liabilities creates a maturity mismatch: the firm must roll its funding repeatedly before the assets pay off, so expansion financed by a rising short-term share of liabilities carries refinancing risk and forced-sale exposure that the market underprices.
considered.reasoning: Maturity structure is an entirely new financing dimension for this archive — every prior signal used the quantity of external capital, none its term — and it is orthogonal to FF5 factors because it does not sort on growth or profitability. Gross PP&E growth pins the investment object to irreversible long-lived capital, which is exactly what makes the mismatch economically binding. The financing leg is a change in the debt-maturity mix, cross-sectionally ranked and demeaned, so firms expanding with stable maturity structure score near zero.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LeveredGoodwillOverhang
considered.hypothesis: The accumulated stock of goodwill measures how much of the balance sheet was built by past acquisitions rather than organic investment; when that acquired base is also financed by above-industry liabilities, the firm has little cushion against impairment, and the eventual write-down and covenant pressure are not priced in advance.
considered.reasoning: This is a stock-versus-stock interaction rather than yet another flow interaction: it asks whether the legacy of externally funded expansion, not this year's transaction, is what the market misprices, which is a temporal concept the archive has not tested. Industry-z-scoring leverage removes the sector component that would otherwise make this a distress sort, and goodwill scaled by assets is a stable, slow-moving measure that should give unusually persistent portfolio composition — a direct remedy for the unstable, high-turnover legs of prior flow-based designs. COALESCE encodes the economically correct convention that a firm reporting no goodwill has none.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: InorganicTiltLeveredUp
considered.hypothesis: Holding total investment scale fixed, a firm that buys growth rather than builds it and simultaneously steps up its liability ratio is levering the balance sheet to acquire assets it did not have to earn — the empire-building configuration — whereas the same inorganic tilt executed without a leverage step-up reflects genuine surplus funding capacity.
considered.reasoning: The investment leg is no longer an investment level (which is why the previous version reduced to acquisition-growth times debt-issuance, two published anomalies): it is the composition of investment — the acquisition rank minus the capex rank — so total investment intensity is differenced out and the sort is on build-versus-buy at given scale. The financing leg is likewise a mix change (the year-over-year move in liabilities to assets), not an issuance quantity, so the signal cannot be a rescaling of net external financing, and it sidesteps the payment-method literature entirely because the claim concerns balance-sheet leverage taken on around the deal rather than cash versus stock consideration. Re-ranking the composition difference keeps the weight non-negative so the interaction stays monotone, and both legs come from high-coverage items.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LiquidityExhaustedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, ppent), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(TS_MAX(che, 5), che), at), 1), WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is not whether investment is externally financed but whether the firm has any funding capacity left: a heavy reinvestor whose cash balance has been drained far below its five-year peak while its liability ratio climbs has exhausted both internal and external slack, so any operating disappointment forces asset sales or dilution and equity absorbs the loss.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the hiring-times-issuance ablation for a different economic construct — funding-capacity exhaustion — built from a distance-from-extreme temporal measure (cash drawdown from its own five-year maximum) combined with the direction of the liability ratio, neither of which is a published quantity-of-financing anomaly. The mechanism predicts underperformance through financial fragility rather than through overvaluation, so the spread's factor loadings should differ from the CMA/RMW-dominated equity-issuance designs that produced perverse FF5 alphas in earlier generations. The financing composite is demeaned, so a heavy reinvestor with intact liquidity and stable leverage sits in the middle of the sort, keeping the test on the interaction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: UnstableFinancingBackedInvestment
considered.hypothesis: Sustained investment programs require dependable funding; a firm whose leverage policy lurches from year to year has stop-go access to outside capital, so its investment is exposed to interruption and its projects are more likely to be abandoned mid-stream, which equity holders underprice.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the operator-only conjunction test with a second-moment financing channel that the archive has never used — the five-year volatility of the change in the liability ratio — so the content is the reliability of funding rather than its level or direction, and it cannot be a restatement of net-external-financing results whose signal is a first moment. Financing instability is plausibly unrelated to CMA and RMW loadings, giving the FF5 spread a route to survive factor adjustment where level-based issuance sorts were absorbed. Investment intensity enters as a bounded non-negative rank weight and the volatility leg is rank-transformed before demeaning, so neither leg's tail can dictate decile membership.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RolloverExposedCapacityBuild
considered.hypothesis: Capacity expansion becomes dangerous when the funding must be rolled before the assets produce cash and the firm holds no liquid buffer to repay it; the joint state of a short-maturity liability structure and thin cash relative to liabilities is genuine rollover exposure, which the market underprices in expanding firms.
considered.reasoning: ShortDebtFundedCapacity is the only archive signal with FMB and FF5 alpha both correctly signed, but it used only the one-year change in the maturity mix, which is a noisy flow; this replaces it with the maturity mix level plus a liquidity-buffer channel, so the gate measures the actual refinancing state rather than its increment. Maturity structure and liquidity coverage are dimensions FF5 does not span, which is why this family produced correctly signed alphas where equity-issuance designs did not. Scaling cash by liabilities rather than assets makes the buffer measure directly comparable to the obligation it must cover.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: HiringOnAStretchedBalanceSheet
considered.hypothesis: Adding headcount is an irreversible fixed-cost commitment; when it is undertaken by a firm that is levered above its industry norm and holds little cash, the firm has no buffer to carry the payroll through a demand shortfall, so the expansion converts directly into distress risk borne by equity.
considered.reasoning: This crosses the archive's strongest cross-sectional investment object (employment growth, fmb -4.53 in HiringFundedByOutsideCapital) with the financing state family that alone has produced correctly signed FF5 alphas, a combination never tested — the earlier hiring signal used share-count growth and debt-ratio change, i.e. Family A flows, which is exactly why its alpha was +0.007. Industry-z-scoring the leverage level strips the sector-distress component the critic warned about, leaving firm-specific stretch, while the cash channel adds the buffer dimension. If the joint objective is attainable anywhere, it should be where a high-FMB investment channel meets a high-alpha financing state.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: GoodwillBoughtOnCredit
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), at), 1)), ZSCORE(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(lt, at), LAG(RATIO(lt, at), 3)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: An accumulated goodwill base is only a warning sign if the deals that created it were paid for by borrowing; goodwill built by a firm whose leverage ratio is no higher than three years ago was funded out of earnings or equity and carries no comparable overhang.
considered.reasoning: This is a deliberate decomposition of the archive's best alpha: replacing the leverage level with the three-year change in leverage tests directly whether that result reflects a static distress sort (the critic's concern) or the debt-funded acquisition history the hypothesis actually claims. A three-year window matches the horizon over which an acquisition program is financed and keeps the gate a slow-moving, low-turnover variable, preserving the stable portfolio composition that made the goodwill signal's t-statistic reliable. If the alpha survives with the level replaced by the accumulation, the mechanism is funding source; if it collapses, the archive result should be reinterpreted as leverage sorting.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: InvestingAtOwnLeveragePeak
considered.hypothesis: Firms differ permanently in how much debt they can carry, so what reveals externally funded overexpansion is not a high leverage ratio but investing while leverage sits at the top of the firm's own five-year range: the firm has exhausted the debt capacity it normally operates with, and the marginal project is being financed beyond its self-imposed limit.
considered.reasoning: The gate is a within-firm time-series position rather than a cross-sectional level, so a chronically levered utility with stable policy scores at the middle while a historically conservative firm that has just pushed to its own record leverage scores at the top — this is precisely the dimension a plain net-leverage or lt/at sort cannot express and it removes the industry/distress re-sorting the critic identified in the earlier version. Because TS_RANK is uniform on [0,1] by construction it is bounded and tie-free, which should give the interaction a more nearly linear cross-sectional relation with returns and hence an FMB slope, the missing half of the Family B evidence. Investment intensity enters as a bounded non-negative weight, so low investors sit near zero regardless of their debt history.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: UnsecuredBorrowingForCapex
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ppegt, at), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Debt-financed investment is benign when the firm owns a large pledgeable capital base and dangerous when it does not: borrowing to invest with little tangible collateral means creditors are lending against future cash flows, so the debt is priced to a soft state of the world and any shortfall triggers refinancing failure that equity absorbs.
considered.reasoning: The gate is collateral quality interacted with the debt flow, not the acquisition-versus-capex composition times a leverage step-up that already failed as InorganicTiltLeveredUp; the investment object here is organic capex and the new economic content is the pledgeability of the asset base, a dimension no archive signal has used. Gross PP&E over assets is a stable, high-coverage tangibility measure, and inverting its rank before combining with net debt issuance means the gate is high only for low-collateral borrowers, low for tangible-asset borrowers, and neutral for firms not borrowing. Collateral scarcity is not spanned by CMA or RMW, giving the spread a route to survive FF5 adjustment in the way the Family B designs did.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BorrowedDistributionsWhileExpanding
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), at), 1)), SUB(MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dvt, prstkc), at), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 1))), MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dvt, prstkc), at), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 1))))))
considered.hypothesis: Distributions signal internal funding capacity only when they are not accompanied by rising liabilities; an expanding firm that pays out heavily while levering up is financing its distributions with creditors' money, which depletes the balance sheet while presenting a shareholder-friendly appearance.
considered.reasoning: The additive SUMRANK gate was the flaw the critic identified — it let high-payout deleveragers and low-payout leveragers score alike — so the gate is now an explicit conjunction: MIN of the payout rank and the leverage-increase rank, minus the mirror conjunction of payout with leverage reduction, which is positive only for genuinely borrowed distributions and negative only for genuinely self-funded ones. Low-payout firms score near zero in both terms and fall in the middle, so the sort cannot be driven by the payout main effect whose univariate sign runs the other way. The whole gate is bounded in [-1, 1] and multiplied by a bounded investment weight, so decile membership is stable and no skewed ratio can dominate.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: InventoryOnShortMoney
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(invt, 1), at), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dlc, lt), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Inventory accumulated on short-dated credit with no cash buffer is the most fragile form of expansion: the goods must be sold before the credit matures, so a demand shortfall forces distressed markdowns to raise the cash the balance sheet does not hold.
considered.reasoning: DebtFundedInventoryBuild failed (fmb 0.23, alpha +0.013) with a liability-versus-equity growth gate that the critic warned was noisy for small book equity; replacing it with the rollover-fragility state tests directly whether the gate, not the investment object, was the binding weakness. Working capital is a distinct investment object from the capacity and labor objects behind the two archive winners, so a correctly signed alpha here establishes that the fragility mechanism is general rather than specific to gross PP&E, while a failure localizes it to irreversible fixed capital. Inventory change scaled by assets is well populated and continuous, aiding decile stability.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LastResortEquityFundedGrowth
considered.hypothesis: Equity-funded growth is not uniformly bad news: a cash-rich issuer is raising capital opportunistically from a position of strength, whereas an issuer whose cash cannot cover its liabilities is diluting shareholders because it has no alternative, and only the latter should underperform on a risk-adjusted basis.
considered.reasoning: Every equity-issuance design in the archive produced a strong negative FMB slope but a zero or perverse FF5 alpha (IssuanceIntoCashNotCapex reached +0.032, t 3.16) because cash-rich, high-issuance growth firms dominate the long leg and their loadings on CMA and RMW already explain their low raw returns; adding the liquidity-buffer condition removes exactly that population from the long leg. This is the one test in the batch that could deliver both strong cross-sectional and portfolio evidence, because it retains the channel that drives FMB slopes and adds the channel that drives alphas. Asset growth is used as the investment object to keep the expansion measure broad and comparable to the classic externally funded growth anchor.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CapexBurstOnFragileBalanceSheet
considered.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, at), 5), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dlc, lt), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is not that a firm is capital-intensive but that it is spending at the top of its own recent range while its funding structure is fragile; a firm at a five-year high in reinvestment with short-dated debt and no cash is stretching precisely when it can least afford a shortfall.
considered.reasoning: Cross-sectional capex intensity largely reflects industry capital intensity, so the weighting leg in the archive's winners may be proxying for asset-heavy sectors rather than for an expansion decision; replacing it with a within-firm time-series position removes the sector component while leaving the fragility gate untouched, which cleanly attributes the alpha to firm-level expansion timing versus industry composition. TS_RANK is bounded and uniform, so this also mildly addresses the flat-FMB problem without changing the economics of the gate. If the alpha survives, the mechanism is a decision-level overextension story; if it disappears, the archive result depends on capital intensity and should be industry-adjusted going forward.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashCoverageOfInvestmentSpend
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0))), 1))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dlc, lt), 1), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(lt, at), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: The economically meaningful measure of self-funding is how many years of the firm's own investment programme its cash balance can pay for; a firm whose liquid assets cover only a fraction of one year of spending must return to capital markets on schedule, and if its liabilities are also short-dated and above industry norms it will do so from a position of weakness.
considered.reasoning: Rather than stacking every fragility channel into one gate, this restructures the interaction so each economic dimension appears exactly once: cash now enters the weighting leg as a coverage ratio of the investment programme (a genuine funding-need-versus-internal-funds construct, not a spending level), while the gate carries only debt structure and industry-relative leverage. That makes the design discriminating rather than a union of tested gates — if it works, the operative variable is the ratio of internal funds to committed spending, which no archive signal has measured, and cash is no longer double-counted across the two legs. Ranking the coverage ratio handles firms with negligible investment (huge coverage, low weight) and firms with zero cash (low coverage, high weight) without denominator blow-ups.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WithinIndustryRolloverExpansion
considered.hypothesis: If rollover-exposed expansion is a firm-level funding-fragility effect, it should hold among direct competitors; if instead the archive result reflects sector composition — cash-poor, short-funded industries such as retail and transport being sorted against cash-rich technology and pharmaceutical firms — then removing the industry mean will destroy it.
considered.reasoning: Unlike a terminal monotone rank, industry z-scoring genuinely reshuffles decile membership and therefore changes the FF5 alpha, the Sharpe ratio and the FMB slope, so this is a substantive test of what the archive's strongest result (alpha -5.9%, t -5.35) actually is. Cash holdings and debt maturity structure are strongly industry-determined, making this the single most important robustness question for the direction the search has converged on. Industry demeaning also removes a large common component of cross-sectional variation, which typically raises both the cross-sectional slope's precision and the hedged spread's Sharpe if the underlying effect is firm-specific.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MaturityWallWithoutMarketAccess
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), at), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dlc, ADD(che, dlc)), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(dltis, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: An expanding firm is in trouble when debt falling due within the year exceeds the cash it holds and it is simultaneously not raising new debt — the maturity wall is real, the liquidity to meet it is absent, and the absence of fresh issuance shows the credit market is not refinancing it, so investment must be funded by retrenchment or dilution.
considered.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that dltr is realised retirement, ambiguous in sign because it accompanies routine rollover; this replaces it with dlc, the debt actually contracted to mature within one year, expressed as the bounded share of near-term obligations not covered by cash, which is unambiguous in direction and free of denominator instability. The second channel adds a credit-access dimension new to the archive: low gross debt issuance relative to existing liabilities indicates the firm is not being refinanced, which turns a maturity wall into a binding constraint rather than a scheduling detail. Both channels are ranked before demeaning so the gate is neutral for firms with covered maturities or normal issuance activity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: FragilityWeightedExpansionTilt
considered.hypothesis: Among firms whose funding structure is fragile — short-dated liabilities and no liquid buffer — the ones expanding capacity should underperform the ones shrinking it, because fragility is only destructive when the firm is committing capital it may not be able to finance to completion.
considered.reasoning: This is the identification test the critic has repeatedly demanded: the roles of the two legs are swapped, so fragility becomes the non-negative weight and expansion the demeaned conditioning variable, which means the long leg is fragile expanders and the short leg is fragile contractors while robust firms sit in the middle. Decile membership changes completely relative to every archive signal, so the outcome is informative either way: a large negative alpha establishes that the investment decision matters within fragile firms, while a null result would show the family's -5% alphas are a financial-constraints state effect and future refinement should stop dressing it as an investment interaction. Both legs are bounded and rank-based, so the reversed construction does not introduce tail sensitivity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EquityRaisedToRepayCreditors
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: When a firm issues equity while simultaneously paying down debt, the new shareholders' money is not funding the investment programme at all — it is funding creditors, which reveals that lenders have withdrawn support and that management is diluting shareholders under duress rather than to exploit an opportunity.
considered.reasoning: Every archive design treated equity and debt financing as substitutable measures of external dependence; this one exploits their *joint configuration*, and the combination of dilution with net debt retirement is a distinct economic state — a creditor-driven recapitalisation — that no prior signal can express. It keeps investment intensity as the weighting leg so the claim remains about how expansion is funded, and it should inherit the FMB power of the issuance channel while adding a duress dimension that is not a growth-firm characteristic and hence not spanned by CMA or RMW. Scaling net debt issuance by total liabilities makes the deleveraging channel comparable across firm size and debt capacity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PayoutCutFundedCapacityBuild
considered.hypothesis: A firm that expands capacity while cutting its distributions and holding no liquidity is financing growth by withdrawing cash from shareholders under constraint; the payout cut is the tell that internal funds are insufficient and that the expansion is being pushed through against the firm's financial capacity.
considered.reasoning: Prior payout-based designs (SelfFundedMinusExtFundedInvest, BorrowedDistributionsWhileExpanding) treated the *level* of payout as evidence of self-funding and failed; this instead uses the *direction of change* in distributions as a revealed-preference signal about internal funding adequacy, which is a different economic claim and pairs naturally with the liquidity channel that has driven the archive's alphas. Dividend reductions are informative precisely because they are costly and reluctant, so combining them with expansion identifies firms stretching beyond their means rather than firms that simply do not pay dividends. Non-payers cluster at zero change and therefore sit in the middle of the gate rather than contaminating either leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SupplierFinancedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, DELTA(invt, 1)), at), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Not all external funding comes from investors: a firm can finance fixed and working capital growth by stretching its suppliers and other operating creditors, and expansion paid for by rising non-debt liabilities in a firm with no liquid buffer is the least durable form of external funding because trade credit is withdrawn first when performance disappoints.
considered.reasoning: This introduces a funding source the archive has never measured — operating liabilities, computed as total liabilities net of interest-bearing debt — instead of tweaking the horizon of the share-issuance channel that the critic correctly identified as already tested. The investment leg deliberately combines capex and inventory build because trade credit funds precisely this joint fixed-plus-working-capital expansion, and the accrual-like character of stretched payables is a dimension FF5 does not span, which is where the archive's alphas have come from. The liquidity channel is retained as the second gate component because it is the one ingredient repeatedly shown to convert this family's spreads into risk-adjusted alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DilutedGrowthLeverageGate
considered.hypothesis: If dilution-funded growth underperforms because the issuer is genuinely constrained, then industry-relative indebtedness should substitute for the cash-shortfall channel; if instead the operative constraint is specifically the absence of liquid assets, replacing cash with leverage will destroy the alpha even though both are standard constraint proxies.
considered.reasoning: The expansion leg and the dilution channel are now byte-identical to the archive's jointly strongest signal (LastResortEquityFundedGrowth: fmb -3.83, alpha -4.3%, t -3.71), so exactly one thing changes — che/lt is replaced by industry-z-scored lt/at — making any difference in the statistics attributable to the constraint channel alone, which repairs the confounded design the critic rejected. The answer directs the remaining generations: if leverage substitutes freely, the mechanism is debt overhang and slow-moving leverage states are the right refinement axis; if it does not, precautionary-liquidity exhaustion is the mechanism and cash-based measures should be the sole focus. Industry demeaning of leverage is retained because raw lt/at was previously shown to sort partly on sector distress.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: GrowthWithoutCollateralOrCash
considered.hypothesis: Ex-ante funding capacity, rather than realised issuance, determines whether expansion is sustainable: a firm growing its balance sheet while owning little pledgeable capital and holding no liquid buffer cannot finance a shortfall from either collateral or cash, so its growth is the most likely to be halted or refinanced on punitive terms.
considered.reasoning: The mechanical coupling the critic identified is removed: expansion is now measured as total asset growth rather than growth in the same net PP&E base that appears in the collateral ratio, and collateral is measured with gross PP&E over assets, so neither leg shares a small-denominator artefact with the other. The signal contains no realised financing flow at all, which distinguishes it from every other proposal in this batch and isolates capacity from behaviour — the cleanest available test of whether the archive's alphas reflect constraint states or funding actions. Both gate channels are slow-moving stocks, so portfolio composition should be stable and the ls_talpha correspondingly reliable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LiquidationCoverageDilutedGrowth
considered.hypothesis: A firm's ability to fund an expansion without going back to the market depends on everything it can turn into cash — liquid balances plus pledgeable physical capital — measured against what it already owes; diluting shareholders while that coverage is thin is the true mark of externally dependent expansion.
considered.reasoning: Two channels have independently produced -4% to -5% alphas in this archive, liquidity shortfall (che/lt) and collateral scarcity (low ppegt/at), and rather than stacking them as separate gate terms this merges them into one economically meaningful coverage ratio: liquid plus pledgeable assets over total liabilities. That keeps the gate two-dimensional (funding capacity and dilution) instead of a kitchen sink, while strictly improving the measurement of capacity relative to the winner's cash-only denominator. The dilution channel is retained unchanged because it is the archive's only reliable source of cross-sectional slope, so this is a targeted upgrade of the one design that scored on both criteria.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DollarEquityIssuanceIlliquidGrowth
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), lt), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: The economically relevant quantity is how many dollars of outside equity the firm actually took in net of what it returned, not how much its share count drifted; net equity raised relative to the liabilities it must service measures genuine external dependence, and it should predict more sharply than share-count growth for an illiquid expander.
considered.reasoning: Share-count growth conflates stock splits, small option exercises and genuine capital raising, so replacing it with the cash-flow-statement net equity issuance (sstk minus prstkc) is a measurement upgrade of the winner's FMB-generating channel while holding the expansion weight and liquidity channel fixed, making the comparison interpretable. Scaling by total liabilities rather than assets expresses the raise in the same units as the obligations that make external funding necessary, aligning both gate channels on one denominator. If this strengthens the slope without harming the alpha, the last generations should build the funding channel from dollar flows rather than share counts.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PostIssuanceCashBurnExpansion
considered.hypothesis: The most exposed expander is the one that raised outside equity a year ago and has since burned through the proceeds while continuing to grow: the money is gone, the growth commitments remain, and another dilutive raise is imminent on whatever terms the market offers.
considered.reasoning: Every prior design measured dilution and liquidity contemporaneously and therefore cannot distinguish a firm that just banked fresh capital (temporarily liquid and safe) from one that has spent it; using lagged issuance with the current-year *change* in liquidity coverage makes the sequence explicit and identifies the burn-through state. This is a genuinely dynamic reformulation rather than a horizon tweak, because the two channels now refer to different dates and the sign of the second channel is a direction of travel, not a level. It also predicts a specific, testable ordering: the state should be more informative than either contemporaneous channel if the mechanism is anticipated future dilution.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: HiringDilutionIlliquidity
considered.hypothesis: Payroll is the least deferrable commitment a firm makes, so a workforce expansion undertaken by a diluting, illiquid firm creates the most acute future funding requirement — wages must be paid monthly whether or not the capital markets cooperate.
considered.reasoning: Headcount growth is the archive's strongest cross-sectional selection variable (fmb -4.53) and the dilution-plus-illiquidity gate is its strongest joint gate, yet the two have never been combined: the earlier hiring signals used either issuance-plus-debt flows (alpha +0.007) or leverage-plus-cash levels (alpha -5.4% but fmb -0.07). Because labor commitments are recurring rather than one-off, the funding-need selection logic established in generation 5 applies more forcefully here than for capex or asset growth. If both statistics come in strong this becomes the leading candidate, and if only the alpha survives it confirms that the slope comes from the dilution channel interacting with balance-sheet growth specifically.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AboveIndustryGrowthOnOutsideMoney
considered.hypothesis: Growing at 20% in an industry growing at 25% is not overexpansion; empire building is expansion in excess of what peers are doing, so the selection device should be industry-relative growth, which isolates managerial aggression from sector-wide demand.
considered.reasoning: This changes only the selection device, replacing raw asset growth with its industry-demeaned counterpart, so any improvement is attributable to removing sector demand conditions from the definition of aggressive expansion — an economic refinement rather than a rescaling, since decile membership shifts substantially. Generation 4 showed industry demeaning preserves this family's alphas, which makes it safe to apply on the selection side where it has clearer economic meaning than on the gate side. Holding the gate fixed keeps the batch internally comparable: Signals 1 and 2 test gate measurement, Signals 4 through 6 test the selection device, and Signal 3 tests timing.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MultiYearCapacityProgramOnOutsideMoney
considered.hypothesis: Ongoing funding need is created by a multi-year capacity build still in progress, not by capital intensity: a firm whose gross capital stock has expanded cumulatively over three years has committed to projects that must be completed, so if it is also diluting shareholders and holding no liquid buffer it will have to return to the market on whatever terms are available.
considered.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that a moving average of (capx+aqc)/at is a level of capital intensity that sorts on industry technology rather than on expansion; replacing it with three-year cumulative growth in gross PP&E makes the selection device unambiguously an expansion measure, scale-free and comparable across capital-intensive and asset-light firms. The economic content of the change is horizon-of-commitment rather than smoothing: a single year's growth may reflect a completed project with no residual funding requirement, whereas a three-year build identifies programmes still consuming capital, which is exactly the population in which the dilution-plus-illiquidity gate should bite hardest. The gate is held identical to the archive's jointly strongest signal so the result is attributable solely to the selection device, and gross PP&E is reported continuously, so the longer window costs little coverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ExcessGrowthOnDollarOutsideEquity
considered.hypothesis: Empire building is expansion in excess of what peers are doing, funded with dollars raised from new shareholders by a firm whose cash cannot cover its obligations; combining the industry-relative expansion selector with the dollar issuance measure should identify that configuration more precisely than either refinement alone.
considered.reasoning: Two independently validated generation-6 improvements have never been combined — industry-demeaned expansion (alpha -4.4%, t -3.51) and dollar net equity issuance (fmb -4.73, alpha -4.6%) — and each addressed a different element of the architecture, so the combination has a genuine chance of dominating both. Scaling issuance by assets rather than liabilities repairs the instability the critic flagged for near-debt-free firms while leaving the cash-coverage channel on its liabilities denominator, where it has repeatedly delivered alpha. COALESCE on both flow items encodes the correct convention that an unreported issuance or repurchase line means none occurred, which should restore the coverage lost by the sparser cash-flow variables.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: TotalOutsideFundingIlliquidGrowth
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(dltis, 0)), ADD(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(dltr, 0))), at), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: What matters for an illiquid expander is the total quantity of outside money absorbed, whether it comes from shareholders or lenders, because both create claims that must be serviced from cash the firm does not yet generate.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested equity-only and debt-only funding channels separately but never the total dollar external financing flow inside the cash-coverage gate that generates the alpha, so this determines whether the equity specificity of the current leader is essential or whether the effect is about outside capital in general. If the total flow strengthens the slope without weakening the alpha, the final generations should standardise on it; if it dilutes the result, the mechanism is specifically dilution-driven market timing rather than generic external dependence. Using assets as the common denominator keeps the two funding sources comparable and avoids the small-liability instability of the current leader's scaling.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NetLiquidityBufferDilutedGrowth
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Cash already committed to debt maturing within the year is not a buffer; the true funding cushion of an expanding firm is cash net of near-term debt, measured against everything it owes, and that net measure should discriminate more sharply than gross cash.
considered.reasoning: The gate's cash-coverage level is the single element that produces this family's FF5 alphas, and the two failed generation-6 variants showed it is sensitive to exactly how capacity is defined — adding collateral destroyed it and differencing it destroyed it — which makes a disciplined, economically motivated refinement of the numerator the highest-value remaining test. Subtracting debt in current liabilities from cash uses the rollover channel that independently produced -5.9% alpha in the archive, but embeds it inside the coverage level rather than adding a separate gate term, avoiding the kitchen-sink problem. All other elements are held identical to the current leader, so the result is attributable to the buffer definition alone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ChronicOutsideEquityDependence
considered.hypothesis: External equity dependence is a standing condition rather than an event: a firm that has taken in net equity in each of the last three years while holding no liquid buffer has a business model that does not self-fund, and its expansion is far more likely to destroy value than that of a firm making one opportunistic raise.
considered.reasoning: The archive has established that the *level* of cash coverage beats its change, which raises the symmetric question for the funding channel — whether a persistent dollar-issuance state beats a single-year flow — and answering it determines the horizon on which the surviving signal should be built. A three-year average of dollar issuance is a genuine state variable rather than a smoothing tweak, because chronic and episodic issuers with the same current-year flow are economically different firms, and it also cuts turnover, which should support the ls_talpha. Coverage should hold up because the flows are COALESCEd to zero when unreported, so the window does not require three consecutive non-missing issuance lines.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EquityTiltedFundingOfExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(dltis, 0), COALESCE(dltr, 0)), at)), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Holding the amount of outside money fixed, a firm that chooses to fund expansion by selling shares rather than by borrowing is revealing that it regards its equity as expensive currency for outsiders and cheap for itself — the market-timing configuration — and that choice should predict worse returns than debt-funded expansion of the same size.
considered.reasoning: Every archive design measured the quantity of external funding; this measures its composition as the equity-minus-debt tilt, which nets out to zero for a firm raising equally from both sources and therefore cannot be a restatement of the composite-issuance or external-financing anomalies. It provides the pecking-order counterpart to Signal 2: read together, the pair separates "how much outside money" from "which kind", which is the sharpest remaining economic question in the theme's market-timing story. The cash-coverage gate is retained because it is what converts these spreads into FF5 alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LeontiefDilutionIlliquidityGate
considered.hypothesis: Last-resort external funding is a joint condition, so the gate should be limited by whichever condition is *least* satisfied: a firm scoring at the top only because it raised a large amount of equity, while still holding ample cash, is not funding-constrained, and neither is a cash-poor firm that raised nothing.
considered.reasoning: The critic's algebra is correct for the symmetric two-MIN form, so the mirror term is dropped and the gate is a single Leontief minimum, which is genuinely not a monotone transform of SUMRANK — a firm at the 99th percentile of issuance and the 40th percentile of illiquidity ranks far below the additive gate's assessment, so decile membership changes materially. Everything else is held identical to the archive leader's architecture (asset-growth selector, dollar net equity issuance, cash-to-liabilities level), making this a clean test of whether the mechanism is a corner phenomenon requiring both conditions or a pair of substitutable constraints. If the conjunction sharpens the alpha and Sharpe, the final generation should adopt the Leontief gate; if it weakens them, additivity is the correct functional form and the search can close on the existing leader.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EveryYearIssuerExpansion
considered.hypothesis: True external-equity dependence means the firm went to the market in *every* recent year, not that a single large raise pulled up its average; the minimum annual net issuance over three years identifies firms that cannot fund themselves in any year, and their expansion should be the most suspect.
considered.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that a three-year mean cannot distinguish one large raise from three small ones, and TS_MIN answers exactly that objection: it is high only when net issuance was positive and material in each of the three years, making "chronic" a logical rather than an averaged condition. Because a firm that repurchased in any single year is pushed to the bottom of the channel, the short leg fills with firms demonstrating at least episodic self-funding, sharpening the self-funded versus externally funded contrast at the heart of the theme. Everything else matches the archive leader, so this isolates the definition of persistence.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OutsideMoneyBeyondInvestment
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(dltis, 0)), ADD(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(dltr, 0))), at), RATIO(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), at)), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: When a firm raises more outside capital than it spends on capital expenditure and acquisitions, the excess is not funding growth at all — it is covering operating cash burn — and expansion financed this way reflects a business that cannot pay its own running costs, let alone earn a return on new assets.
considered.reasoning: This is the one genuinely new economic state in the batch: prior designs measured the quantity, currency, persistence and timing of external funding, but never whether the money raised exceeded the investment it was supposedly raising for, which separates loss-funding from project-funding within the population of externally financed expanders. Both components are asset-scaled flows so the difference is well behaved and free of the small-denominator problems that sank earlier ratio designs. Because the illiquidity gate is retained unchanged, a strong result would show the family's alpha can be sharpened by identifying *what the money was used for*, a direction the final generation could then refine.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EscalatingMarketDependence
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), MA(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 3)), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Dependence that is escalating is more informative than dependence that is merely present: a firm raising materially more outside equity this year than its own three-year norm, while holding no liquid buffer, is losing control of its funding trajectory — the raise is being forced by the shortfall rather than chosen from strength.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested the level of issuance (generation 6), its persistence (generation 7) and its lagged value (generation 6), but never its position relative to the firm's own funding norm, which is a different economic claim: chronic issuers with a stable policy are priced by investors who expect it, whereas an unexpected step-up in recourse to the market reveals new information about cash adequacy. Because the escalation channel is firm-normalised it is close to orthogonal to the cross-sectional issuance level that already drives the archive's slope, so a strong result would show the two are complementary rather than substitutable. The illiquidity level is retained unchanged because generation 6 established that only the level, not the change, of cash coverage produces FF5 alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ExpansionWithNoSelfFundingRecord
considered.hypothesis: The credible certificate of self-funding is a sustained record of paying cash out to owners; a firm that has distributed nothing over three years and holds no liquid buffer has never demonstrated that its operations generate surplus cash, so its expansion must be financed by outsiders whether or not an issuance appears in this year's accounts.
considered.reasoning: Every strong archive signal identifies external funding by the *presence of a realised financing flow*; this identifies it by the *absence of any evidence of internal funding*, which is a different and untested identification strategy that catches firms funding growth through operating liabilities, leases or off-cycle raises that issuance flows miss. It also repairs the generation-5 payout designs, which used the level or the one-year change in distributions and were dominated by the tied mass of non-payers, by using a three-year distribution record where the zero group is economically meaningful rather than a measurement artefact. The liquidity channel is retained so that cash-rich non-payers — firms that could distribute but choose to retain — are not misclassified as dependent.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PaperGrowthOnOutsideMoney
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(GROWTH(at, 1), GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: What the outside money buys matters: a balance sheet inflating faster than the productive capital stock means the expansion is going into receivables, inventories, goodwill and financial assets rather than into capacity, and such growth funded by new shareholders in an illiquid firm is the least likely to earn a return.
considered.reasoning: The selector is changed in kind rather than in measurement: instead of asking how fast the firm is expanding, it asks whether expansion is outrunning the productive base, so capital-intensive builders funded externally are separated from firms whose assets are growing in soft, non-productive form. This is the complement of OutsideMoneyBeyondInvestment — that signal asks whether the money exceeded investment spending, this one asks whether the asset growth was productive — and together they test the "use of proceeds" dimension from two independent angles. Both growth rates are scale-free and continuously reported, so the selector is well populated and does not inherit the small-base coupling problem that sank the earlier collateral design.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BufferAtItsOwnHistoricLow
considered.hypothesis: Target cash holdings are firm-specific — set by business model, volatility and industry — so the informative condition is not that a firm holds less cash than other firms but that it holds less than it normally holds itself: an expanding, issuing firm whose liquidity coverage is at the bottom of its own five-year range has exhausted the buffer it deliberately maintains.
considered.reasoning: Cross-sectional cash-to-liabilities is heavily determined by industry and business model, so the archive's gate may be sorting on permanent firm type rather than on a binding funding condition; a within-firm position measure discriminates between a chronically lean retailer operating normally and a firm that has drawn its own buffer to a multi-year low. This is a different economic claim from the failed InvestingAtOwnLeveragePeak, because leverage is a slow policy target whereas the cash buffer is the margin firms actually manage quarter to quarter, and because generation 6 showed the *change* in coverage fails while the level works — a within-firm rank is a level concept, not a difference. TS_RANK is bounded and uniform, keeping the gate free of tail sensitivity while the issuance channel preserves the cross-sectional slope.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NonCashExpansionOnOutsideEquity
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(SUB(at, che), 1), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: An equity raise mechanically inflates total assets through the cash it deposits, so total asset growth partly measures the financing event rather than any expansion; growth in non-cash assets is the real commitment of capital, and it is that real expansion, when funded by outsiders and unbuffered by liquidity, which should predict poor returns.
considered.reasoning: Every archive design pairs an issuance channel with an asset-growth selector without noticing that the two are linked by construction — the cash proceeds sit inside the selector — so purging cash from the expansion measure removes a tautological component and should sharpen rather than weaken the interaction. This is a substantive identification fix, not a rescaling: firms that raised capital and parked it in cash (whose FF5 alpha the archive showed runs the *wrong* way, IssuanceIntoCashNotCapex +3.2%) drop out of the long leg, which is precisely the contaminating population. Both legs remain high-coverage balance-sheet items, so coverage should match the 0.132 leaders.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DilutionWithoutPerShareAccretion
considered.hypothesis: Issuance is not harmful in itself — it is harmful when the capital raised fails to raise the book value attributable to each existing share; an expanding, illiquid firm whose book equity per share is falling is growing at its current owners' expense.
considered.reasoning: This changes what the funding channel identifies: instead of the quantity of outside money taken in, it measures whether that money accreted or destroyed per-share owner value, so firms that issue at fair or favourable terms are separated from those diluting existing holders. The construct was tried once in generation 1 but inside a failed architecture (paired with a dividend-change channel and no cash gate, alpha 0.000); testing it within the now-validated selector-plus-illiquidity architecture is a genuine re-examination rather than a repeat, and it addresses the critic's standing concern that the archive's funding channel is close to the published net-issuance anomaly. Book equity per share is high coverage, and NEG orients falling accretion to the long leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: IndustryRelativeLiquidityGate
considered.hypothesis: Required liquidity is set by the business a firm is in — a software company needs a cash pile a grocer does not — so the binding constraint is holding less cash than industry peers, which is measurable, rather than less than the firm's own past, which generation 8 showed is not informative.
considered.reasoning: This is a targeted repair of a diagnosed failure: BufferAtItsOwnHistoricLow replaced the cross-sectional cash level with a within-firm position and the alpha flipped to +0.7%, which could mean either that firm-relative normalisation is wrong or that any normalisation destroys the signal — industry demeaning sits precisely between the two and distinguishes those explanations. It also directly tests the critic's long-standing concern that the cash-coverage gate may be sorting on permanent industry type rather than on funding capacity: if the alpha survives industry demeaning, the mechanism is firm-specific constraint, and if it collapses, the archive's headline results should be reported as partly sectoral. Everything else is held at the leader's specification so the attribution is unambiguous.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ReplacementBurdenedExpansionOnOutsideEquity
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm with a heavily depreciated capital base must fund replacement as well as growth, so the same headline expansion implies a far larger future capital requirement when net-to-gross PP&E is low; expanding on an old asset base while raising outside equity with no liquid buffer is the most acute funding-need configuration.
considered.reasoning: Rather than re-parameterising the coverage denominator — which the critic rightly notes the gate is insensitive to — this introduces an entirely new dimension the archive has never used: capital vintage, measured as net over gross PP&E, which determines how much of tomorrow's spending is non-discretionary replacement rather than optional growth. It is placed in the selector, whose established job since generation 5 is to identify firms with inescapable funding needs, leaving the validated funding gate untouched so attribution is clean. Vintage varies substantially within industries and both inputs are continuously reported, so this is neither a sector proxy nor a coverage risk.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: HardOperatingAssetBuildOnOutsideEquity
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(ADD(ppent, invt), 1), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: The assets that create an unavoidable financing requirement are the physically committed ones — plant in service and goods on the shelf — because they cannot be liquidated at short notice or written off without loss; growth in that hard operating base, funded by new shareholders in a firm with no liquid buffer, is externally funded expansion in its most binding form.
considered.reasoning: This is a definitional change to what counts as expansion, not a persistence device: total assets include cash, receivables, goodwill and financial assets, all of which either come from the raise itself or can be released, whereas plant plus inventory is the committed, illiquid core that must be financed to completion and carried through a downturn. It therefore differs economically from both the asset-growth selectors and the non-cash-asset selector, and it unifies the two investment objects that produced the archive's strongest portfolio evidence (gross PP&E growth, alpha -5.9%; inventory build, alpha -5.7%) into the single balance-sheet quantity they jointly measure, rather than pairing best-performing legs. Both components are high-coverage and slow-moving, which should support a stable sort and a reliable ls_talpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: GoodwillCreatedOnFreshEquity
considered.hypothesis: Acquisition-driven expansion is the theme's headline empire-building mechanism: goodwill newly created on the balance sheet measures how much scale was bought rather than built, and when that purchase coincides with fresh equity raised by a firm holding no liquid buffer, the deal was funded by outsiders at a price the firm could not otherwise afford.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the payout conjunction the critic identified as a REIT and utility sector proxy and instead revisits the archive's very first deal-based signal, which had a strong slope but a wrong-signed alpha (DealPaymentMethodTilt: fmb -2.81, alpha +1.5%) because its gate was a share-count-versus-cash payment contrast rather than a funding-capacity state — replacing that gate with the now-validated dollar-issuance-plus-illiquidity gate is a direct, interpretable test of whether the deal channel was failing on measurement of financing or on economics. The goodwill increment is used alone, avoiding the cash-outflow double counting flagged in generation 0, and COALESCE encodes the correct convention that a firm reporting no goodwill created none. If it succeeds, the inorganic mechanism at the centre of the empire-building story is finally captured; if it fails, the archive's conclusion is that the effect is organic-expansion-specific.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: This is a product of two ranks of two well-known published anomalies (Cooper-Gulen-Schill asset growth and Bradshaw-Richardson-Sloan net external financing), and the claim that rank-multiplication "isolates the interaction rather than either main effect" is false — the product of two [0,1] ranks is dominated by the two main effects, so the test cannot distinguish the funding-source story from a simple composite of two known signals.

The conditional design is economically sensible and reasonably novel, but the hard indicator gate assigns exactly zero to roughly half the cross-section, piling mass at the median so quantile breakpoints degenerate and portfolio composition becomes unstable, and no ungated benchmark is included to establish that the leverage condition is what matters.

Stock-financed acquirer underperformance is a canonical published result (Loughran-Vijh, Rau-Vermaelen, plus net-share-issuance), and the expression is internally muddled because Compustat aqc records mainly the cash outflow for acquisitions — precisely what stock-financed deals lack — so the numerator mixes a cash-deal proxy with a goodwill proxy that partly double-counts it.

Beyond being a rescaled version of the known XFIN/net-external-financing anomaly, the construction is mechanically unsound: capx+aqc in the denominator is frequently near zero or zero, so extreme deciles will be populated by tiny-denominator firms rather than by the intended funding-mix contrast, and 1% winsorization will not repair a non-monotone ratio of two signed quantities.

This is essentially the multi-year composite-issuance/long-horizon-investment anomaly (Daniel-Titman; Bradshaw et al.) repackaged, and like the first proposal the rank product is driven by the two main effects rather than the claimed interaction, making it a cosmetic horizon variant of ExtFinFundedAssetGrowth rather than a distinct test.

Algebraically the signal reduces to RANK(investment) times a signed payout-minus-issuance rank difference, which is a defensible genuine interaction — investment intensity is differenced out and only funding mix is priced, with the expected positive sign matching the direction — though the bracket alone is close to a known net-payout-yield composite and prstkc appears in both legs, so the incremental content rests entirely on the investment gate and this should be benchmarked against the ungated funding-mix term.

The labor-hiring channel is a substantively different investment object from the archive's capex/asset-growth designs and is not spanned by CMA, and the expression's direction matches the stated hypothesis, though the claim of much higher coverage is dubious since `emp` is sparsely and staledly reported and the hiring-rate anomaly itself is already published (Bazdresch-Belo-Lin), so the incremental content rests entirely on the financing interaction.

Inventory-growth and net-external-financing effects are each published, but conditioning inventory accumulation on liability-versus-equity growth is a coherent and previously untested interaction whose sign convention is internally consistent; watch that GROWTH(ceq) is unstable for firms with small or negative book equity, which can inject noise into the demeaned financing leg.

This is largely a cosmetic re-parameterization of the already-evaluated SelfFundedMinusExtFundedInvest (same investment×payout-versus-issuance structure, rescaled denominators), and the funding leg's dominant component, negative share-count growth, is a direct restatement of the well-documented net share issuance anomaly.

It overlaps materially with the archived InvestFundedByMarketNotCash (issuance plus cash build again flagged as opportunistic), but by putting issuance in the weighting leg it targets the complementary population of non-investing issuers that the earlier signal zeroes out, and the sign is internally consistent.

Direction and construction are internally consistent and the stock-plus-flow leverage state is a genuine addition to the archive's flow-only financing legs, but the lt/at level term will dominate the composite and load heavily on distress/value/profitability, so any surviving FF5 alpha may reflect leverage sorting rather than the risk-shifting mechanism claimed.

The post-financing retrenchment timing is a real economic distinction rather than a horizon tweak and the expression matches the hypothesis, but note the expected negative sign fights the documented capex/investment anomaly (capex-cutters historically earn higher returns), so the interaction must dominate a known opposing main effect for this to work.

The industry-demeaning of the leverage leg plus the switch to a capex/ppent reinvestment rate is a substantive, correctly-diagnosed fix to LeveredCapexOverhang's confounding of firm-specific stretch with sector distress, and the sign logic (high rank × high positive z → low returns) is internally consistent, though the underlying investment-plus-financing channel remains close to well-trodden asset-growth/external-financing territory.

This is a near-mechanical product of two separately published anomalies (acquisition/asset-growth and net external debt financing) and economically overlaps InvestFundedByMarketNotCash restricted to the deal leg, while its expected sign sits awkwardly against the payment-method literature in which cash-financed acquirers underperform *less* than equity-financed ones.

Debt maturity mix is a genuinely new financing dimension for this archive rather than another quantity-of-capital variant, the mismatch story is economically coherent with irreversible gross PP&E growth as the investment object, and the construction (ranked, demeaned change in dlc/lt gating expansion) matches the stated hypothesis and sign.

A stock-versus-stock, low-turnover interaction is a defensible departure from the archive's flow designs and the persistence argument is credible, but the leverage leg risks reducing to a familiar distress sort, goodwill intensity is itself a documented negative predictor, and ZSCORE(IND_ZSCORE(...)) is redundant window dressing.

Replacing one of the two components of HiringFundedByOutsideCapital's funding composite with the other is a narrow ablation rather than a substantively different improvement, and the surviving content is the published hiring-rate anomaly gated by the equally published net-debt-issuance anomaly.

The MIN construction does implement a real conjunction and correctly collapses to zero for low-investment firms (it reduces to an investment-gated 2·rank(net debt issuance)−1), but the economic content is a rediscovery of InvestFundedByMarketNotCash with only the operator changed, making this a construction test rather than a new mechanism.

The gate collapses to a plain net-leverage level, making this a cosmetic re-specification of the already-tested LeveredCapexOverhang / LiquidityExhaustedExpansion family (investment × balance-sheet stretch) rather than a substantively new mechanism, and it risks simply re-sorting on the known leverage/cash-holdings dimensions.

Replacing the noisy one-year maturity-mix change with the maturity-structure level plus a liability-scaled liquidity buffer is a defensible measurement upgrade of the one correctly-signed archive signal, and debt-maturity/rollover exposure is a dimension not spanned by FF5, though it remains within the same family and partly overlaps published short-maturity-debt risk results.

Employment growth is itself a published anomaly (hiring rate), so the novelty rests entirely on the industry-adjusted leverage-plus-low-cash gate, which is coherent with the fixed-cost-commitment story and distinct from the prior hiring signal's issuance flows, but the motivation ("pair the best FMB leg with the best alpha leg") is closer to metric-shopping than to a new economic claim.

Because DELTA(intan) is dominated by acquisition-driven goodwill and purchased intangibles, this is largely the already-tested InorganicTiltLeveredUp configuration (inorganic expansion × leverage step-up, fmb 0.64, alpha +0.007) with a different accounting proxy, so it is a likely rediscovery of a failed design rather than a genuine flow-versus-stock decomposition.

This is a well-posed, falsifiable decomposition that isolates whether the archive's strongest alpha comes from the debt-funded-acquisition mechanism or from a static leverage/distress sort, and the three-year leverage change is a sensibly matched, low-turnover gate rather than a cosmetic tweak.

The hypothesis states a conjunction (high investment AND high payout AND rising leverage), but SUMRANK is additive over two channels with opposite univariate return predictability (payout yield positive, leverage increase negative), so high-payout/deleveraging and low-payout/levering firms score identically and the gate does not compute the claimed "borrowed distributions" configuration.

This is essentially a kitchen-sink union of the exact fragility channels already tested in RolloverExposedCapacityBuild, HiringOnAStretchedBalanceSheet and LiquidityExhaustedExpansion, with an unintended weighting asymmetry from the nested SUMRANK (dlc/lt gets half the gate weight), so it adds no new economics and cannot discriminate whether the gate or the investment leg drives the alpha.

By the proposer's own admission a terminal monotone rank cannot change decile membership or the FF5 alpha, making this a purely cosmetic re-submission of an archive signal whose one informative output (whether FMB improves) is a known property of monotone re-scaling rather than a new hypothesis.

Swapping the failed liability-growth gate for the rollover-fragility state on a genuinely different investment object (working capital) is a coherent and interpretable test of mechanism generality, though it inherits the family's unresolved risk that the fragility gate — essentially a distress/financial-constraints state — is doing all the work independent of the investment leg.

The expression is internally inconsistent with the hypothesis: dltr is realized long-term debt *retired during the year*, not a forward-looking scheduled maturity wall, and high dltr typically accompanies high dltis (rollover scale) or successful deleveraging, so the sign of the obligation channel is ambiguous rather than unambiguously fragile.

The construction matches the stated conditional logic and the diagnosis of why prior issuance signals had perverse alphas is thoughtful, but the design sits very close to the published result that the asset-growth and share-issuance anomalies concentrate among financially constrained firms, so novelty is modest.

Replacing cross-sectional capex intensity with a within-firm five-year TS_RANK is a substantive, well-motivated attempt to strip out industry capital intensity from the weighting leg while holding the gate fixed, giving an interpretable attribution regardless of outcome, though a five-year TS_RANK is coarse and the reused gate keeps this within an already crowded family.

This is a one-parameter horizon tweak (csho growth 1y → 3y) of the archive's LastResortEquityFundedGrowth, with an identical expansion leg, identical liquidity gate and identical economic claim, i.e. precisely the cosmetic variant the objective warns against.

It is a mechanical transpose of RolloverExposedCapacityBuild rather than a new mechanism, but the swap of weight and conditioning roles genuinely changes decile membership and delivers an interpretable ablation of whether the family's −5% alphas come from the investment decision or from the constraint state alone, and the sign logic is internally consistent.

The stated purpose is to isolate which constraint channel (cash vs. leverage) drives the archive alpha, but the proposal simultaneously changes the expansion object from asset growth to net PP&E growth, so any weakening is uninterpretable and the design fails as the diagnostic it claims to be.

The joint configuration of equity issuance with net debt retirement identifies a creditor-driven recapitalisation state that nets out to roughly zero total external financing and is therefore not a rediscovery of the composite-issuance or external-financing anomaly, and the expression's direction matches the stated negative sign.

Using the change rather than the level of distributions as a revealed-preference measure of internal funding adequacy is a defensible new angle relative to the failed payout-level designs, though the large tied mass of non-payers at zero delta will leave the gate driven mostly by the cash leg and dilute the incremental information.

The two legs are mechanically coupled — GROWTH(ppent) is inflated and far noisier precisely for the low-ppent/at firms that the collateral leg ranks as constrained — so the interaction risks capturing a small-base scaling artefact rather than the claimed funding-capacity channel.

A coherent and interpretable merge of the archive's two working gate channels (cash coverage and collateral) into a single liabilities-scaled capacity ratio while holding the dilution leg fixed, though it is a one-leg substitution on the existing winner and the use of *gross* PPE as "pledgeable value" is a crude proxy that will tilt the gate toward capital-intensity levels rather than true funding capacity.

Replacing share-count growth with cash-flow-statement net equity issuance is a genuine measurement improvement that removes splits and option-exercise noise, the sign logic is internally consistent, and scaling both gate channels by liabilities is economically motivated rather than cosmetic — though the (sstk−prstkc)/lt ratio will be unstable for near-debt-free firms even after winsorization.

This is the only proposal in the batch that changes the economic state being identified rather than the measurement of an existing one — lagged issuance combined with a deteriorating liquidity-coverage *change* isolates the burn-through firm from the freshly funded one — and the expression's direction matches the stated hypothesis, with the caveat that a level-plus-change hybrid gate may weaken the portfolio sort relative to the archive's level-based gate.

A three-year moving average of (capx+aqc)/at is a *level* of capital intensity, not an expansion measure, so it will sort largely on persistent industry capital-intensity rather than on funding need, and the change amounts to a smoothing tweak whose main claimed benefit (lower turnover) is a cosmetic rather than economic refinement of the existing winner.

The combination of the archive's strongest cross-sectional selector (headcount growth) with its strongest joint gate has genuinely not been tested and the fixed-cost-commitment logic is sound, but it is still a single-leg swap on the winner and the two prior hiring signals both delivered strength on only one of the two metrics, so the prior on a joint win is modest.
